source_text: Hane fidem annuntians Johannes Domini discipulus, volens per Evangelii annuntiationem auferre eum, qui a Cerintho inseminatus erat hominibus errorem, et multo prius ab his qui dicuntur Nicolaite, qui sunt vulsio ejus quee falso cognominatur ut confunderet eos, et suaderet quoniam unus Deus qui omnia fecit per Verbum suum ; et non, quemadmodum illi dicunt, alterum quidem fabricatorem, alium autem Patrem Domini: et alium quidem fabricatoris filium, alterum vero ®de superioribus Christum, quem et impassibilem perseverasse, descendentem in Jesum filium fabricatoris, et iterum revolasse in suum Pleroma: et Tinitium quidem esse monogenem; Logon autem verum filium unigeniti: et eam conditionem quze est secundum nos, non a primo Deo factam, sed a virtute aliqua valde deorsum subjecta, et abscissa ab eorum communicatione quze sunt invisibilia et innominabilia. Omnia igitur talia cireumscribere volens discipulus Domini, et ' regulam veritatis constituere in Ecclesia, quia est unus Deus omnipotens, qui per Verbum suum omnia fecit, et visibilia et invisibilia; significans quoque, quoniam per Verbum, per quod Deus perfecit conditionem, in hoe et salutem his qui in conditione sunt preestitit hominibus; sic inchoavit in ea que est secundum Evangelium doctrina: Jn principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum: hoc erat in principio apud Deum. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Quod factum est, in ipso vita erat, et vita erat lua hominum, et lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebre eam non comprehenderunt. Omnia, inquit, per ipsum facta sunt ; in omnibus ergo est et hzee quae secundum nos est conditio: non enim concedetur eis, omnia dici ea que sunt infra Pleroma ipsorum. Si enim et hee Pleroma ipsorum continet, non extra est tanta ista conditio, quemadmodum ostendimus in eo libro qui ante hune est ; si autem extra Pleroma sunt heec, quod quidem impossibile visum est, jam non est omnia Pleroma ipsorum: non est ergo extra heee tanta conditio. Abstulit autem a nobis dissensiones omnes ipse Johannes, dicens: In hoc mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit. In sua propria venit, et sui eum non receperunt. Secundum autem Marcionem et eos qui similes sunt ei, neque mundus per eum factus est ; neque in sua venit, sed in aliena, Secundum autem quosdam Gnosticorum, ¢ab angelis factus est iste mundus, et non per Verbum Dei. Secundum autem eos qui sunt a Valentino, iterum non per eum factus est, sed per Demiurgum. Hic enim operabatur similitudines tales fieri, ad imitationem eorum que sunt sursum, quemadmodum dicunt: Demiurgus autem perficiebat fabricationem conditionis. Emissum enim dicunt eum a matre Dominum et Demiurgum ejus dispositionis quee est secundum conditionem, per quem hune mundum factum volunt: cum Evangelium manifeste dicat, quoniam per Verbum, quod in principio erat apud Deum, omnia sunt facta: quod Verbum, inquit, caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. 8. Secundum autem illos, neque Verbum caro factum est, neque Christus, neque qui ex omnibus factus est Salvator. Htenim Verbum et Christum nec advenisse in hune mundum volunt: Salvatorem vero non incarnatum neque passum; descendisse autem quasi columbam in eum Jesum qui factus est ex dispositione, et cum annuntiasset incognitum Patrem, iterum ascendisse in Pleroma. Incarnatum autem et passum quidam quidem eum qui ex dispositione sit dicunt Jesum, quem per Mariam dicunt pertransisse, quasi aquam per tubum: alii vero ° Demiurgi filium, in quem descendisse eum Jesum qui ex dispositione sit: alii rursum Jesum quidem ex Joseph et Maria natum dicunt, et in hune descendisse Christum qui de superioribus sit, sine carne et impassibilem exsistentem. Secundum autem nullam sententiam heereticorum, Verbum Dei caro factum est. Si enim quis regulas ipsorum omnium perscrutetur, inveniet quoniam sine carne et impassibilis ab omnibus illis inducitur Dei Verbum, et qui est in superioribus Christus. Alii enim putant manifestatum eum, quemadmodum hominem transfiguratum; neque autem natum, neque incarnatum dicunt illum: alii vero neque figuram eum assumsisse hominis; sed quemadmodum columbam descendisse in eum Jesum, qui natus est ex Maria. Omnes igitur illos falsos testes ostendens discipulus Domini, ait: Ht Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. Et ut non inquiramus, cujus Dei Verbum caro factum est, ipse insuper docet, dicens : Fuit homo missus a Deo, erat ei nomen Johannes: hic venit in testimonium, ut testaretur de lumine. Non erat ipse lumen, sed ut testaretur de lumine. Preecursor igitur Johannes, qui testatur de lumine, a quo Deo missus est? Utique ab eo cujus Gabriel est angelus, qui etiam evangelisavit generationem ejus; qui et per prophetas promisit angelum suum missurum ante faciem Filii sui, et preeparaturum viam ejus, hoc est, testificaturum de lumine, i spiritw et virtute Helie. Helias autem rursus cujus Dei servus et propheta fuit? Ejus qui fecit coelum et terram, quemadmodum et ipse confitetur. A conditore igitur et fabricatore hujus mundi missus Johannes, quemadmodum poterat testificari de eo lumine, quod ex his que sunt innominabilia et invisibilia descenderit ? Omnes enim heeretici decreverunt, Demiurgum ignorare eam que sit super eum virtutem, cujus testis et ostensor invenitur Johannes. Propter hoc Dominus plus quam prophetam dixit eum habuisse. Reliqui enim omnes prophetze annuntiaverunt adventum paterni luminis; concupierunt autem digni esse videre eum quem preedicabant: Johannes autem et preenuntiavit similiter sicut alii, et advenientem vidit et demonstravit, et credere in eum suasit multis, ita ut ipse et prophete et apostoli locum habuerit.
pass_a_gloss: John, the Lord's disciple, announcing this faith, wanting to remove the error that was sown in people by Cerinthus, and much earlier by those who are called Nicolaites, who are a false offshoot, so that he might confuse them and persuade them that there is one God who made all things through His Word; and not, as they say, one creator and another Father of the Lord: and one son of the creator and another Christ from above, who is impassible and remained, descending into Jesus, the son of the creator, and again returning to His Pleroma: and the Only-begotten is one thing; the true Word is the only-begotten Son: and the condition that is according to us was not made by the first God, but by some power far below and cut off from their communication, which is invisible and unspeakable. Therefore, the Lord's disciple, wanting to circumscribe all such things and establish the rule of truth in the Church, because there is one God, all-powerful, who made all things, visible and invisible, through His Word; also signifying that through the Word, through which God perfected the condition, in this He also provided salvation for those who are in the condition; thus he began in the doctrine that is according to the Gospel: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word: this was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made. What was made, in Him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. All things, he says, were made through Him; therefore, this condition that is according to us is also in all things: for it will not be granted to them that all things are what are below their Pleroma. For if their Pleroma also contains these things, this condition is not outside, as we showed in the previous book; but if these things are outside the Pleroma, which is impossible, then their Pleroma is not all things: therefore, this condition is not outside. But John himself removed all dissensions from us, saying: He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, and the world did not know Him. He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him. According to Marcion and those who are like him, neither was the world made through Him, nor did He come to His own, but to another's. According to some Gnostics, the world was made by angels, and not through the Word of God. According to those who are from Valentinus, the world was not made through Him, but through the Demiurge. For the Demiurge, they say, made the creation of the condition, working such likenesses to imitate those things that are above, as they say. But the Gospel clearly says that all things were made through the Word, which was in the beginning with God, and that the Word became flesh and dwelled among us. According to them, however, the Word did not become flesh, nor did Christ, nor the Savior who was made from all things. For they do not want the Word and Christ to have come into this world; but the Savior, they say, did not become incarnate or suffer, but descended like a dove into Jesus, who was made from the condition, and after announcing the unknown Father, ascended again into the Pleroma. But some say that Jesus, who is from the condition, was incarnate and suffered, whom they say passed through Mary like water through a pipe; others say that the Demiurge's son was in whom Jesus, who is from the condition, descended; others say that Jesus was born from Joseph and Mary, and that Christ, who is from above, without flesh and impassible, descended into Him. But according to no heretical opinion, the Word of God became flesh. For if one examines the rules of all of them, he will find that the Word of God is introduced by all of them as without flesh and impassible, and that Christ, who is above, is such. For some think that He was manifested like a transfigured man; but they do not say that He was born or became incarnate; others say that He did not take on human form, but descended like a dove into Jesus, who was born from Mary. Therefore, the Lord's disciple, showing all these to be false witnesses, says: The Word became flesh and dwelled among us. And so that we may not ask whose Word became flesh, he himself also teaches, saying: There was a man sent from God, whose name was John: he came as a witness, to testify about the light. He was not the light, but he came to testify about the light. Therefore, the precursor John, who testifies about the light, was sent by which God? Certainly by the God whose angel Gabriel is, who also announced His generation; who also promised through the prophets to send His angel before the face of His Son, and to prepare the way for Him, that is, to testify about the light, in the spirit and power of Elijah. And Elijah was the servant and prophet of which God? Of the One who made heaven and earth, as he himself confesses. Therefore, John was sent by the founder and creator of this world, as he was able to testify about the light that descended from those things that are unspeakable and invisible. For all heretics have decreed that the Demiurge is ignorant of the power that is above him, of which John is found to be a witness and revealer. On account of this, the Lord said that he had more than a prophet. For all the other prophets announced the coming of the paternal light; they desired to be worthy to see the One they preached; but John both announced similarly to the others and saw the One who was coming and showed Him and persuaded many to believe in Him, so that he himself held the place of both prophet and apostle.

The Word became flesh and dwelled among us

pass_b_english: John, the Lord's disciple, proclaims this faith in order to uproot the error that Cerinthus sowed among people, and earlier still the error of the so-called Nicolaitans—a counterfeit offshoot that confuses them. He writes to persuade them that one God made all things through His Word, not one Creator and another Father of the Lord, as they claim (John 1:1). They teach two sons: one begotten of the Creator, another Christ from above who remained impassible, descended into Jesus the Creator's son, and then returned to His Pleroma. They distinguish the Only-begotten from the true Word, the only-begotten Son, and insist that our material condition was fashioned not by the first God but by a lower power severed from the invisible, unnameable realm. To fence off all such teachings and fix the rule of truth in the Church, John grounds everything in the one Almighty God who created all things, visible and invisible, through His Word (John 1:1). He also shows that through the very Word by which God perfected creation, He provided salvation for those who live in that creation. So John opens his Gospel doctrine: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was with God in the beginning. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made. What was made in Him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it" (John 1:1). John insists, "All things were made through Him"; therefore this condition of ours also falls within "all things." The heretics cannot restrict "all things" to what lies inside their Pleroma. If their Pleroma contains these things, then our condition is not outside it—as the previous book demonstrated. If our condition lies outside their Pleroma, then their Pleroma is not "all things," which is impossible. Hence our condition is not outside. John himself removes every dispute: "He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, yet the world did not know Him. He came to His own, and His own people did not receive Him" (John 1:10–11). Marcion and his followers deny both that the world was made through Him and that He came to His own; they say He came to another's realm. Some Gnostics claim angels made the world, not God's Word. Valentinians say the Demiurge made it, not the Word. They teach that the Demiurge fashioned creation as a likeness of the things above, but the Gospel declares plainly that all things were made through the Word who was with God in the beginning, and that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). In their systems, however, neither the Word, nor Christ, nor the Savior composed of all things became flesh. They refuse to admit that the Word and Christ entered this world. The Savior, they say, did not become incarnate or suffer, but descended like a dove into Jesus—who sprang from their lower condition—announced the unknown Father, and then ascended back to the Pleroma. Some say Jesus of that lower condition was incarnate and suffered, passing through Mary like water through a pipe. Others say the Demiurge's son received the Jesus from that condition. Others say Jesus was born of Joseph and Mary, and the impassible, fleshless Christ from above descended into Him. But by no heretical opinion did the Word of God become flesh. Examine all their rules and you will find that every one presents God's Word as fleshless and impassible, and the Christ above as likewise. Some imagine He appeared only as a transfigured man, yet deny He was born or incarnate. Others deny He took human form at all, saying He descended like a dove into Jesus born of Mary. Thus the Lord's disciple exposes them all as false witnesses and declares: "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). Lest anyone ask whose Word became flesh, John himself answers: "There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came as a witness to testify concerning the light, so that through him all might believe. He himself was not the light, but came to testify about the light" (John 1:6–8). The forerunner John, who testifies to the light—by which God was he sent? Surely by the God whose angel is Gabriel, who announced John's own birth and promised through the prophets to send His messenger before His Son's face to prepare His way—that is, to testify to the light in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17). And Elijah—servant and prophet of which God? Of the One who made heaven and earth, as Elijah himself confesses (1 Kings 18:36). Therefore John was sent by the Founder and Creator of this world. How else could he bear witness to the light that descended from the invisible, unnameable realm? All heretics decree that the Demiurge is ignorant of the power above him, yet John is found to be that power's witness and revealer. For this reason the Lord said John was more than a prophet (Luke 7:26). All the other prophets announced the coming of the Father's light and longed to see the One they preached. John not only announced Him like the rest, but saw Him coming, pointed Him out, and persuaded many to believe in Him—so that he holds the office of both prophet and apostle.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions of the Latin text regarding the various heretical views (Cerinthians, Nicolaitans, Marcionites, Valentinians, etc.) and the Johannine defense. Scripture citations in Pass B are correctly added to the quoted/alluded clauses (e.g., John 1:1, 1:10-11, 1:14, Luke 1:17, 1 Kings 18:36, Luke 7:26) and match the content. Pass A and B are consistent with the Latin source.
